note.text:
A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Each atom puts in one electron and both atoms count the pair, so both complete their outer shells.
• Single bond: one shared pair (H–H, Cl–Cl). Double bond: two pairs (O=O). Triple bond: three pairs (N≡N).
• Number of bonds an atom forms = electrons it needs to complete its shell: H 1, Cl 1, O 2, N 3, C 4.
• Covalent substances are made of molecules: H₂, O₂, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, CO₂.
Dot-and-cross diagrams show the shared pairs in the overlap of the two atoms' outer shells.

sections.heading: Sharing instead of transferring
sections.text:
Two non-metal atoms both want to gain electrons, so neither will give electrons away. Instead they share.
Each atom puts one electron into a pair that sits between the two nuclei. The shared pair is attracted by both nuclei: that is the covalent bond.
Both atoms count the shared electrons as their own, so both complete their outer shells.

sections.heading: How many bonds?
Dot-and-cross diagrams
sections.text:
Draw the outer shells of the atoms overlapping. Put the shared pairs in the overlap: one electron as a dot (from one atom) and one as a cross (from the other).
Electrons that are not shared are lone pairs. In water, oxygen has two shared pairs and two lone pairs: {8} electrons in all.

worked_example.problem: Show how a molecule of methane, CH₄, is held together.
steps: Carbon ({2}, {4}) needs {4} more electrons; each hydrogen needs {1}.
Carbon shares one pair with each of {4} hydrogen atoms.
Carbon now has {8} outer electrons and each hydrogen has {2}: all shells are full.
worked_example.answer: Four single covalent bonds (four shared pairs)

cards.idea: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons.

cards.idea: An atom forms as many bonds as the electrons it needs.
Two pairs make a double bond; three pairs a triple bond.

e: H–H is single.

pick.q: In a covalent bond, the shared electrons come from…
e: There is no metal in a covalent bond.
Electrons are outside the nucleus.

pick.q: In a dot-and-cross diagram of water, how many electrons are in the outer shell of oxygen?
pick.r: 8 (two shared pairs and two lone pairs)
e: Count the shared electrons too.
That is hydrogen's shell.
Oxygen's second shell holds at most 8.
pick.y: The shared pairs complete oxygen's octet.

pick.q: How many lone (non-bonding) pairs are on the nitrogen atom in ammonia, NH₃?
e: Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons; 3 are used in bonds.
Only 2 electrons are left over: one pair.
Three electrons are used in bonding.

pick.q: Why does hydrogen form only one covalent bond?
pick.r: Its only shell is full with two electrons
e: Hydrogen has one electron.
Its first shell holds only two.
In covalent bonds it shares, not loses.
pick.y: One shared pair gives hydrogen two electrons, like helium.
